The bullish narrative argued that structurally higher defence and nuclear spending could support a Fair Value of £14.5. The bearish view pointed to a Fair Value of £7.5. It focused on the risk that UK and European budget pressure, plus roughly £200 million of zero margin Type 31 revenue each year, could cap revenue growth at 4.7% and keep profit margins closer to 5.9% by 2028.

The clearest new fact for Babcock International Group was the H2 2026 earnings print. Revenue reached £2,639.1m while net income came in at £41.9m. That pulled net margin down to 1.6% compared with 4.9% in H2 2025, which challenged the bullish margin and earnings trajectory more than it supported the cautious revenue view.

The key assumption here was not just higher defence and nuclear spend, but how much of that would turn into profit. When assessing another contractor, focus on whether net margin is moving toward or away from the margin embedded in the original thesis.
